title: Security & Governance Checklist for Generative AI

meta.description: Standards-aligned policy and implementation guide for secure, compliant AI adoption with practical checklists and SOPs.

commitment_devices: Adopt an AI Acceptable Use Policy with mandatory annual signature.
Mandate quarterly AI risk and compliance reviews with results published to all engineering and product leadership.
incentive_design: Reward teams that complete AI deployments with zero critical findings in their go-live audit.
Implement a 'three-strikes' policy for repeat, deliberate violations of the AI Acceptable Use Policy, escalating from manager notification to HR review.
loss_aversion_and_defaults: Default to 'deny' for any use of PII, PHI, or PCI data in public or third-party generative AI tools unless a formal exception and data protection impact assessment (DPIA) is completed.
Implement minimum-privilege roles (e.g., 'AI-ReadOnly', 'AI-Developer', 'AI-Auditor') and enable Row-Level Security (RLS) by default on all data stores used for AI model training or fine-tuning.
social_proof_and_signaling: Publish a company-wide AI compliance dashboard showing key metrics like audit pass rates, training completion, and risk mitigation velocity to signal the norm of secure and responsible use.
Formally recognize 'AI Security Champions' embedded within product and engineering teams to act as peer leaders and evangelists for best practices.

sections.heading: Introduction: The Imperative for AI Governance
sections.summary: This document establishes the official policy, standards, and implementation guidance for the secure, compliant, and responsible use of Generative AI within our organization. It provides a comprehensive framework to manage risks related to data privacy, security, fairness, and operational stability while enabling innovation. Adherence to this guide is mandatory for all employees, contractors, and affiliates involved in the development, deployment, or use of AI systems.
sections.content_markdown:
Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) presents a paradigm shift in how we create, innovate, and operate. From accelerating software development to transforming customer engagement, the potential benefits are immense. However, this power is accompanied by a new class of risks that, if left unmanaged, can lead to severe financial, legal, and reputational damage. Data breaches, privacy violations, algorithmic bias, and erosion of customer trust are not theoretical threats; they are active risks that demand a proactive and structured governance framework.

This guide is built upon internationally recognized standards and best practices, including the  NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)  and  ISO/IEC 42001 . It is designed to be a living document, adaptable to the rapid evolution of AI technology and the regulatory landscape. Its primary objective is to empower our teams to leverage AI confidently and responsibly by providing clear, actionable controls and processes. By embedding security and ethics into the foundation of our AI initiatives, we can ensure that our use of this transformative technology aligns with our core values and long-term strategic goals.

sections.heading: 1. Governance Foundations
sections.summary: This section establishes the core governance structure for AI. It defines the policies for using public vs. private models, outlines the roles and responsibilities through a RACI matrix, and provides a clear risk taxonomy to ensure consistent risk assessment and management across the organization.
sections.content_markdown: Effective AI governance begins with a clear and unambiguous foundation. Before any team can build, fine-tune, or even use a generative AI model, we must establish the rules of engagement. This section lays that groundwork, providing the essential policies and structures needed to ensure that all AI activities are aligned with our organization's risk tolerance and strategic objectives. It answers the fundamental questions of *what* is permissible, *who* is responsible, and *how* we classify and prioritize risks.

subsections.subheading: 1.1 Public vs. Private LLM Policy (p4, e1)
subsections.content_markdown:
The choice between using a public, third-party Large Language Model (LLM) service (e.g., OpenAI's GPT series, Anthropic's Claude) and a private, internally-hosted or self-managed model is the most critical initial decision from a security and privacy perspective. Public models offer convenience and cutting-edge capabilities but introduce significant data privacy risks, as any data sent to them may be used for model training or be subject to the vendor's data handling policies. Private models offer maximum control over data but require significant investment in infrastructure and expertise.

 Policy Snippet: AI Model Usage Tiers 

>  Tier 1: Public/Third-Party AI Services (Default Deny for Sensitive Data) 
> The use of any public or third-party generative AI tool is  prohibited  for any purpose involving company-classified 'Confidential' or 'Restricted' data, including but not limited to Personally Identifiable Information (PII), Protected Health Information (PHI), Payment Card Industry (PCI) data, source code, financial reports, and strategic plans. A formal risk assessment and exception must be approved by the AI Governance Council for any deviation. All interactions with approved public tools must be routed through the central AI Gateway for logging and filtering.

>  Tier 2: Private/Internally-Managed AI Models 
> Internally hosted or managed models (e.g., open-source models deployed in our secure cloud environment) are the  required  choice for all use cases involving 'Confidential' or 'Restricted' data. All such deployments must adhere to the data protection, access control, and logging standards outlined in this document.

subsections.subheading: 1.2 RACI for AI Oversight and Approvals
subsections.content_markdown: Clear accountability is non-negotiable. An AI Governance program without defined ownership is destined to fail. The following RACI (Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed) matrix defines the roles and responsibilities for key AI governance activities. This structure ensures that decisions are made by the right people, with the right input, at the right time. It creates a clear path for approvals and escalations, preventing ambiguity and delay.

A shared understanding of risk is essential for effective governance. This taxonomy, aligned with the  NIST AI RMF  and the  OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications , provides a common language for identifying, assessing, and communicating AI-related risks. Each risk is categorized and defined, with clear severity levels based on potential impact and likelihood. This enables teams to prioritize mitigation efforts and allows leadership to make informed decisions about risk acceptance.

sections.heading: 2. Data Protection and Access Controls
sections.summary: This section details the mandatory controls for protecting data throughout the AI lifecycle. It provides specific standards for handling sensitive data types (PII/PHI/PCI), patterns for implementing granular access controls like Row-Level Security, and requirements for secure secrets management and key rotation.
sections.content_markdown: Data is the lifeblood of generative AI. It is also our most sensitive asset and our greatest liability. The controls in this section are non-negotiable and form the bedrock of our AI security posture. They are designed to enforce the principles of  'Data Protection by Design and by Default'  as mandated by regulations like GDPR. Every stage of the AI lifecycle, from data collection and preparation to model training and inference, must be governed by these data protection standards. Failure to do so not only violates this policy but also breaks the law and the trust of our customers.

subsections.content_markdown:
The presence of Personally Identifiable Information (PII), Protected Health Information (PHI), or Payment Card Industry (PCI) data in any AI workflow triggers the highest level of security requirements. These data types are governed by strict legal and regulatory frameworks (e.g., GDPR, CCPA, HIPAA, PCI-DSS) that carry severe penalties for non-compliance.

 Policy Snippet: Prohibited Data in AI Training 

> The use of raw, unanonymized PII, PHI, or PCI data for the purpose of general model training or fine-tuning is  strictly prohibited . All such data must undergo a certified anonymization or pseudonymization process before it can be introduced into a training dataset. The process and its effectiveness must be documented in a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) and approved by the Data Privacy Officer.

For inference, any system that processes sensitive data must use tokenization or other forms of data masking where possible. If sensitive data must be displayed in an output, it must be masked by default and only revealed based on the user's explicit, role-based permissions.

The principle of  least privilege  dictates that a user or system should only have access to the specific data required to perform its function. In the context of AI, this means tightly controlling access to the underlying data stores used for training and inference. Row-Level Security (RLS) is a database feature that provides a powerful mechanism to enforce this principle. It allows us to define policies that control which rows of data a user can see based on their role or attributes.

 Implementation Pattern: RLS for Multi-Tenant AI Applications 

Consider an AI-powered analytics tool that serves multiple client organizations. An RLS policy on the central data warehouse would ensure that when a user from 'Client A' queries the AI, the underlying query to the database can *only* access rows where the `client_id` column equals 'A'. This is not just an application-level check; it is enforced directly by the database, providing a robust security boundary. All data access roles for AI systems must be defined with the minimum necessary permissions, and access reviews must be conducted quarterly.

AI systems, like any other application, require secrets: API keys, database credentials, encryption keys, etc. These secrets must never be hardcoded in source code, configuration files, or prompt templates. All secrets must be stored and managed in an approved secrets management service, such as  AWS Secrets Manager ,  Azure Key Vault , or  Google Cloud Secret Manager .

 Policy Snippet: Secrets Management 

> All secrets used by AI applications, including API keys for model providers and credentials for data stores, must be managed via the corporate-standard secrets management service. Access to secrets must be granted via IAM roles with the minimum required permissions. All secrets must be configured for automatic rotation with a maximum rotation period of  90 days .

checklists.title: Data Protection and Access Control Checklist
items: Is all sensitive data (PII, PHI, PCI) identified and classified in the Data Classification Matrix?
Has a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) been completed for any AI system processing sensitive data?
Are all training datasets containing sensitive information properly anonymized or pseudonymized?
Are IAM roles for AI services and users defined according to the principle of least privilege?
Is Row-Level Security (RLS) or an equivalent control implemented on data stores to enforce data segregation?
Are all application secrets (API keys, credentials) stored in an approved secrets management service (e.g., Azure Key Vault, AWS Secrets Manager)?
Are all secrets configured for automated rotation with a period of 90 days or less?
Is data encrypted both in transit (TLS 1.2+) and at rest (AES-256)?
Are access logs for sensitive data stores enabled and retained for a minimum of 180 days?

sections.heading: 3. Bias, Fairness, and Responsible AI
sections.summary: This section provides the framework for addressing the ethical dimensions of AI, focusing on bias and fairness. It outlines methods for detecting and mitigating bias, defines key fairness metrics, establishes a requirement for periodic audits, and provides a due diligence process for selecting third-party models.
sections.content_markdown: An AI system that is secure and private but produces unfair or biased outcomes is a failure. Responsible AI is not an optional add-on; it is a core component of quality and risk management. Biased AI systems can perpetuate and even amplify societal inequalities, leading to discriminatory outcomes, reputational damage, and legal liability. This section establishes our commitment to fairness by providing actionable procedures for auditing, measuring, and mitigating algorithmic bias, aligning with the principles of trustworthy AI outlined in the  NIST AI RMF .

subsections.content_markdown:
Bias in AI systems can be introduced at any stage of the lifecycle. It is crucial to understand the common sources to effectively detect and mitigate it.

*  Data Bias:  The training data may underrepresent certain demographic groups or reflect historical societal biases. For example, a resume screening model trained on historical hiring data may learn to favor candidates from specific backgrounds.
*  Algorithmic Bias:  The choice of model or optimization function can introduce bias. Some algorithms may inadvertently prioritize certain features that correlate with sensitive attributes.
*  Human Bias:  The developers, data labelers, and users of the AI system can introduce their own cognitive biases into the process. This can manifest in how data is collected, how features are engineered, or how model outputs are interpreted and used.

 Detection Strategy:  Teams must use a combination of qualitative and quantitative methods to detect bias. This includes exploratory data analysis to check for demographic imbalances in training data and the use of specialized tools (like Google's What-If Tool or IBM's AI Fairness 360) to test the model's performance across different subgroups.

To manage fairness, we must measure it. There is no single universal metric for fairness; the appropriate choice depends on the specific use case and societal context. Teams must define and justify their chosen fairness metrics before model deployment. Audits must be performed quarterly for high-risk systems.

 SOP: AI Fairness Audit 

> 1.   Define Subgroups:  Identify the relevant demographic subgroups for fairness analysis (e.g., based on race, gender, age).
> 2.   Select Metrics:  Choose and document the primary fairness metric(s) to be used. For example:
>     *  Demographic Parity:  Ensure the model's positive prediction rate is similar across all subgroups.
>     *  Equal Opportunity:  Ensure the true positive rate is similar across all subgroups.
> 3.   Execute Tests:  Run the model against a holdout test dataset and calculate the chosen fairness metrics for each subgroup.
> 4.   Analyze & Report:  Compare the metrics across subgroups. If the disparity exceeds a predefined threshold (e.g., 20% difference), document the finding as a bias issue.
> 5.   Mitigate & Remediate:  If bias is detected, the responsible team must implement a mitigation plan (e.g., re-sampling the training data, applying algorithmic debiasing techniques) and re-run the audit. The system cannot go-live or remain in production with unmitigated critical bias.

When using third-party AI models or services, we are still accountable for their performance and ethical implications. Therefore, a rigorous due diligence process is required before onboarding any new AI vendor or model.

 Policy Snippet: Vendor AI Due Diligence 

> Before procurement or integration of any third-party AI system, the sponsoring business unit must, in partnership with the Security and AI Governance teams, complete a formal due diligence assessment. The vendor must provide satisfactory evidence of their own internal AI governance, security, and ethics programs, including documentation on their data handling practices, bias mitigation strategies, and model transparency (e.g., model cards or datasheets).

checklists.title: Vendor AI Due Diligence Checklist
items: Has the vendor provided a SOC 2 Type II report or equivalent security certification?
Has the vendor provided documentation on their data handling and privacy policies?
Does the vendor contractually commit not to use our data for training their models without our explicit consent?
Has the vendor provided a 'model card' or 'datasheet' detailing the model's intended use, limitations, and performance metrics?
Has the vendor provided evidence of their bias detection and mitigation processes?
Does the vendor provide mechanisms for us to report and address issues of bias or unfairness?
Is the vendor compliant with relevant regulations such as GDPR and CCPA?
Have the legal and data privacy teams reviewed and approved the vendor's terms of service and data processing addendum?

tables.title: Key Fairness Metrics
rows: The likelihood of a positive outcome is the same for all groups. P(prediction=1 | group=A) = P(prediction=1 | group=B)
When the goal is to have the overall proportion of positive outcomes be equal across groups, and the cost of false positives/negatives is low.
The likelihood of a positive outcome is the same for all groups, *given that the true outcome is positive*. P(prediction=1 | true=1, group=A) = P(prediction=1 | true=1, group=B)
When it's crucial to not disadvantage any group that is qualified (avoid false negatives), such as in loan approvals or hiring.
Combines Equal Opportunity (true positive rate) and also requires an equal false positive rate across groups.
When both false positives and false negatives have significant costs and should be balanced across groups, such as in criminal justice risk assessments.

sections.heading: 4. Dev & Deployment Controls
sections.summary: This section specifies the technical controls required for the secure development and deployment of AI systems. It covers the implementation of model gateways for policy enforcement, standards for audit logging, the role of human-in-the-loop, abuse prevention mechanisms, and processes for change management and training.
sections.content_markdown: A well-designed AI model can be rendered insecure by a poorly designed deployment architecture. This section provides the technical guardrails for our MLOps and engineering teams. These controls are designed to create a secure, observable, and resilient environment for our AI applications. They shift security and governance 'left', embedding them into the development lifecycle rather than treating them as an afterthought. Adherence to these controls is mandatory for any AI system to be deployed into a production environment.

subsections.content_markdown:
A  Model Gateway  is a centralized service that acts as a single entry and exit point for all generative AI requests and responses. It is a critical control point for enforcing security policies.

*  Functions of a Model Gateway: 
    *  Authentication & Authorization:  Ensures that only authenticated and authorized users/services can access AI models.
    *  Logging:  Creates a centralized, non-repudiable audit trail of all prompts and responses.
    *  Filtering:  Scans both inputs (prompts) and outputs (responses) for sensitive data, malicious content, and policy violations.
    *  Rate Limiting:  Prevents abuse and denial-of-service attacks.

 Audit Logs  must capture sufficient detail to reconstruct any event. At a minimum, AI audit logs must include: a timestamp, the user/service principal ID, the source IP address, the model being queried, the full prompt, and the full response. Logs must be forwarded to a central SIEM for monitoring and alerting.

 Human-in-the-Loop (HITL)  is a process that requires human intervention for high-stakes decisions. For AI systems that generate content for external use or make critical automated decisions, an HITL workflow is mandatory. This means a qualified human must review and approve the AI's output before it is finalized.

subsections.subheading: 4.2 Rate Limiting, Content Filters, Abuse Prevention
subsections.content_markdown:
Generative AI systems are susceptible to various forms of abuse. We must implement multiple layers of defense to protect them.

*  Rate Limiting:  Implement strict rate limits based on user, IP address, and API key. This helps mitigate brute-force attacks and resource-heavy denial-of-service attempts (OWASP LLM04).
*  Content Filters:  Use automated filters to block prompts and responses containing hate speech, harassment, or other content that violates our Acceptable Use Policy. Additionally, implement PII/PHI detection filters to prevent sensitive data leakage.
*  Input Validation:  Sanitize and validate all user inputs to prevent prompt injection attacks. This includes stripping control characters and implementing length limits.
*  Cost Monitoring:  Set up billing alerts and budget caps on all third-party AI service accounts to get early warnings of runaway costs, which can be an indicator of abuse.

AI models are not static; they are updated and retrained. This process must be governed by a formal change management process.

 SOP: AI Model Change Management 

> 1.   Change Request:  A formal change request must be submitted, detailing the reason for the change (e.g., retraining with new data, updating to a new model version) and the potential impact.
> 2.   Risk Assessment:  The change must be risk-assessed, with a particular focus on potential impacts to fairness, security, and performance.
> 3.   Testing:  The new model version must pass all regression tests, as well as a new fairness and bias audit.
> 4.   Approval:  The change must be approved by the AI Governance Council or their delegates before deployment.
> 5.   Deployment:  The new model is deployed, and its performance is monitored closely.

 Workforce Training:  All employees will be required to complete an annual training module on responsible and secure AI use. This training will cover the key elements of this policy, secure prompting techniques, and how to identify and report potential AI-related risks.

checklists.title: Go-Live Readiness Checklist
items: Has the AI system been registered in the official AI model inventory?
Is the system integrated with the central AI Gateway for all external model calls?
Are comprehensive audit logs being generated and sent to the central SIEM?
Have rate limits and content filters been configured according to policy?
Has a final bias and fairness audit been conducted and passed?
Has the Data Protection and Access Control Checklist been completed and all items addressed?
Has the system undergone a formal security review and penetration test?
Is a Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) process in place for all high-risk outputs?
Is there a documented rollback plan in case of production failure?
Have the responsible teams received training on this policy and the system's operational procedures?

sections.heading: 5. Data Readiness & Lifecycle Management
sections.summary: This section covers the critical processes for managing the data that fuels our AI models. It establishes requirements for data quality and lineage, the use of specialized datasets for testing, and the essential practice of monitoring for model drift and triggering retraining.
sections.content_markdown: The axiom 'garbage in, garbage out' is more relevant than ever in the age of generative AI. The quality, integrity, and management of our data directly determine the performance, reliability, and safety of our AI systems. This section provides the framework for governing the entire data lifecycle, from initial collection to eventual retirement, ensuring our data is fit for purpose and that our models remain accurate and relevant over time. This aligns with the 'Measure' and 'Manage' functions of the  NIST AI RMF .

subsections.content_markdown:
High-quality data is the prerequisite for a high-quality model. Teams must implement automated data quality checks in their data pipelines.

*  Data Quality:  Checks should validate data for completeness, accuracy, consistency, and timeliness. Any data failing these checks must be quarantined for review.
*  Data Lineage:  It must be possible to trace the origin of all data used for training. Data lineage tools must be used to track data from its source system, through all transformations, to the final training dataset. This is critical for auditing, debugging, and fulfilling regulatory requests (e.g., under GDPR's 'Right to be Forgotten').
*  Data Retention:  Data used for AI training, as well as the models themselves, are considered records and must adhere to the corporate data retention policy. A retention schedule must be defined for each AI system, specifying how long training data, models, and audit logs will be stored.

To build robust and secure models, we must test them against a wide range of scenarios, including those not present in our historical data.

*  Synthetic Data:  This is artificially generated data that mimics the properties of real-world data. It can be used to augment training datasets, especially to improve the representation of minority groups to mitigate bias. It can also be used to create test cases for rare or edge-case scenarios.
*  Red-Team Datasets:  This involves creating a specialized dataset of adversarial prompts designed to try and 'break' the model. This is a form of proactive security testing. For example, a red-team dataset for a customer service bot might include prompts designed to elicit confidential information, generate inappropriate content, or execute prompt injection attacks. All high-risk, externally-facing models must undergo red-team testing before deployment.

The real world is constantly changing, and a model trained on past data will gradually become less accurate over time. This phenomenon is known as  model drift . We must actively monitor for it.

*  Concept Drift:  The statistical properties of the target variable change. (e.g., the definition of 'customer churn' changes due to a new product offering).
*  Data Drift:  The statistical properties of the input data change. (e.g., a new demographic of users starts using the product).

 Monitoring and Retraining:  Production models must be continuously monitored for drift. This involves comparing the statistical distribution of live inference data against the training data. Automated alerts must be configured to notify the responsible team when drift exceeds a predefined threshold. This alert is a formal trigger for the model retraining process, which must follow the AI Model Change Management SOP.

checklists.title: Periodic AI System Review Checklist (Quarterly)
items: Have the IAM roles and access permissions for the system been reviewed and re-certified?
Has the model's performance and drift been analyzed? Is retraining necessary?
Has a new bias and fairness audit been conducted? Are there any new biases?
Have the system's audit logs been reviewed for anomalous activity or security events?
Is the system's documentation, including its entry in the model inventory, still accurate?
Are the system's dependencies (e.g., libraries, base model) up-to-date and patched?
Has the business value and ROI of the system been re-evaluated?
Are the data retention policies being correctly applied to the system's data and logs?

tables.title: Model Retraining Triggers
rows: A scheduled, periodic retraining cycle (e.g., quarterly) to incorporate new data and refresh the model.
A product recommendation model is retrained every month with the latest sales data.
Automated monitoring detects a significant statistical shift in the production data compared to the training data.
An alert is fired because the average age of users interacting with a chatbot has dropped significantly.
A fundamental change in the business context makes the old model obsolete.
A fraud detection model needs to be retrained because the company launched in a new country with different fraud patterns.
A periodic audit reveals that the model has developed a bias against a particular group.
A quarterly fairness audit shows a loan application model is now unfairly rejecting a higher percentage of applicants from a certain zip code.

sections.heading: 6. Incident Response and Management
sections.summary: This section outlines the procedures for responding to AI-specific security and ethical incidents. It provides a dedicated incident response workflow for fairness issues and establishes the protocol for managing and learning from AI-related failures.
sections.content_markdown: Even with robust preventative controls, incidents will happen. Our response to these incidents defines our resilience and our commitment to responsible AI. An AI-related incident—whether it's a security breach, a data leak, or a critical fairness failure—must be handled with speed, precision, and transparency. This section adapts our standard incident response framework to address the unique challenges posed by AI systems, such as the need to investigate algorithmic behavior and manage ethical fallout.

subsections.subheading: 6.1 Incident Response Workflow for Fairness Incidents
subsections.content_markdown:
When a fairness audit or a user report indicates that an AI system is producing biased or discriminatory outcomes, it must be treated as a high-severity incident. The standard security incident response process may not be sufficient, as the 'vulnerability' is not in the code but in the model's behavior.

 SOP: AI Fairness Incident Response 

> 1.   Containment:  The first step is to stop the harm. If the bias is severe, the responsible team must immediately disable the AI feature or roll back to a previously known-good version of the model. The decision to disable a feature will be made by the on-call Engineering Lead in consultation with the Product Manager.
> 2.   Triage & Investigation:  The AI Ethics & Compliance team, in partnership with the data science team, will investigate the root cause of the bias. This involves analyzing the model's predictions, examining the training data for imbalances, and attempting to reproduce the reported issue.
> 3.   Remediation:  Based on the investigation, a remediation plan is developed. This may involve collecting more representative data, applying algorithmic debiasing techniques, or adding post-processing rules to correct for bias. The plan must be documented and approved by the AI Governance Council.
> 4.   Recovery & Communication:  Once the remediation is implemented and a new fairness audit is passed, the feature can be re-enabled. A post-mortem report must be written, detailing the incident, the root cause, and the steps taken to prevent recurrence. A communication plan will be developed by the Legal and Communications teams if the incident impacted external users.

Every AI incident is a learning opportunity. A blameless post-mortem process is mandatory for all critical and high-severity AI incidents. The goal of the post-mortem is not to assign blame but to understand the sequence of events and identify systemic weaknesses in our processes or controls. The findings from these post-mortems will be used as direct input to update this governance policy, our technical standards, and our training programs, creating a feedback loop for continuous improvement.

sections.heading: 7. Conclusion and Acknowledgment
sections.summary: This final section summarizes the key principles of the AI governance policy and includes an acknowledgment that all relevant personnel must sign, confirming they have read, understood, and agree to abide by the policies outlined in this document.
sections.content_markdown:
The responsible and secure use of Generative AI is a shared responsibility. While this document provides the framework, its effectiveness depends on the commitment of every individual who develops, deploys, or uses AI in our organization. This policy is not intended to stifle innovation but to enable it by creating a secure and ethical foundation. By adhering to these principles, we can unlock the transformative potential of AI while upholding our commitments to our customers, our partners, and our community. This is a living document that will evolve with the technology and the regulatory landscape, and we welcome feedback for its continuous improvement.

 Acknowledgment of Policy 

*I acknowledge that I have received, read, and understood the organization's 'Security & Governance Policy for Generative AI'. I agree to abide by all the policies, standards, and procedures contained within it. I understand that failure to comply with this policy may result in disciplinary action, up to and including termination of employment or contract.*

sections.heading: 8. Appendices
sections.summary: This section contains supplementary materials, including templates, detailed checklists, and examples to aid in the implementation of the AI governance policy. These resources are designed to be practical tools for our teams.

checklists.title: AI Acceptable Use Policy (AUP) - Key Prohibitions
items: You must not input any 'Restricted' or 'Confidential' data (including PII, PHI, PCI, source code, or financial data) into any public or third-party AI tool without a formal, documented exception.
You must not use company AI systems to generate content that is unlawful, harassing, defamatory, or in violation of the company's code of conduct.
You must not use AI to generate content that infringes on the intellectual property rights of others. Always attribute sources where appropriate.
You must not attempt to bypass security controls, content filters, or logging mechanisms on any company-provided AI tool.
You must critically review all AI-generated output for accuracy and appropriateness before using it for any business purpose. You are accountable for the final work product.
You must report any suspected security vulnerabilities, data leaks, or biased outputs from an AI system to the Security Team immediately.

checklists.title: Secure Prompting Guide - Quick Checklist
items: Never include secrets:  Do not put API keys, passwords, or other credentials in your prompts.
Never include sensitive data:  Do not paste PII, source code, or other confidential information into prompts for public models.
Be specific and provide context:  Clearly define the role, task, and desired format for the AI. This reduces ambiguity and the chance of unexpected outputs.
Instruct the AI on what *not* to do:  Explicitly forbid the AI from making up facts, using certain words, or revealing sensitive information patterns.
Review and edit:  Treat the AI's output as a first draft. Always review for factual accuracy, security issues, and bias before using it.
Beware of 'prompt injection':  Do not build applications that directly concatenate untrusted user input with your core system prompt. Sanitize and separate user input.

prompt_templates.name: Code Review and Security Analysis Prompt
prompt_templates.usage: For developers to get a preliminary security analysis of a code snippet using an approved, privately-hosted LLM. This should not be used with public models.
prompt_templates.template_markdown:
You are an expert security code reviewer. Your task is to analyze the following code snippet for potential security vulnerabilities. Focus on common issues like injection flaws, insecure deserialization, broken authentication, and sensitive data exposure. For each vulnerability you find, provide the following:
